Vishnu. The preserver god of the Hindu trinity, responsible for maintaining cosmic order and protecting the universe from chaos and dissolution.

Vishnu is revered across Hindu traditions as the sustainer of existence and the embodiment of dharma, righteous law. He is known for descending to Earth in multiple avatars, or incarnations, to restore cosmic balance whenever it is threatened by evil or disorder. His role differs fundamentally from Brahma, the creator, or Shiva, the destroyer. Vishnu represents the active force that sustains and renews creation across infinite cycles of time.

Hinduism's largest branch, Vaishnavism, places Vishnu at the center of devotional practice. This tradition celebrates his earthly incarnations, particularly Krishna and Rama, as direct experiences of the divine. Vishnu embodies the principle that cosmic order must be actively maintained and defended against the forces of chaos.

As the second member of the Trimurti, Vishnu works alongside Brahma and Shiva. He maintains the cosmos across infinite cycles of yugas, ages that cycle eternally. When one cycle ends in destruction, he preserves and sustains through the next creation. His role is essentially active and engaged, unlike the transcendent Brahma or the meditative Shiva. Vishnu engages directly with the world to preserve dharma.

In his iconography, Vishnu is depicted with four arms and blue skin, symbolic of infinity and the endless sky. He holds a chakra, a discus of power, and a conch, which represents the sound of creation. He is often shown reclining on Shesha, the cosmic serpent that symbolizes eternity, in the cosmic ocean. From his navel emerges a lotus bearing Brahma, the creator.

Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth, fortune, and abundance, is Vishnu's eternal consort. She appears at his side in most depictions. When Vishnu rides into the world, he does so on Garuda, the divine eagle, who serves as his mount and celestial vehicle in his active interventions on Earth.

Vishnu has innumerable avatars across cosmic history, the most celebrated being the ten Dashavatara. Krishna, his eighth avatar, is the protagonist of the Bhagavad Gita and embodies divine love, or bhakti, and righteous action, or karma yoga. Rama, his seventh avatar and hero of the Ramayana, embodies the perfect king and righteous dharma in human form. Lesser avatars include Parasurama, the warrior sage; Narasimha, the lion-man who defeated demons; and in some traditions, Buddha himself.

Vaishnavism, the largest branch of Hinduism, prioritizes devotion to Vishnu and his avatars as the path to liberation, known as moksha. The Bhagavad Gita is central to this tradition, for it is the text in which Krishna, Vishnu's avatar, instructs the warrior Arjuna on dharma, duty, and the nature of action itself. Devotees seek a personal relationship with Vishnu through meditation, chanting his names as mantras, and living righteous lives.

Vishnu represents a distinctive Hindu theological emphasis: the idea that the divine must be actively engaged with the world to sustain it. This contrasts sharply with many religious traditions in which transcendence requires withdrawal from the world. Vaishnavism is a theology of divine engagement and care. His avatars, especially Krishna and Rama, became the focus of some of Hinduism's most beloved devotional literature and philosophy.

The concept of divine incarnation through avatars created theological space for Hindu syncretism with Buddhism. It allowed Buddha himself to be incorporated as a Vishnu avatar, bridging two great traditions of Asia. In modern Hinduism, Vishnu worship continues to anchor devotional practice for millions of people. His festivals, Janmashtami for Krishna and Rama Navami for Rama, remain among the most significant Hindu celebrations. His emphasis on sustaining cosmic order, dharma, has resonated with contemporary Hindu thinkers addressing ethics and social responsibility.
